passage: I'm Manjula, and I live in the flat below Devika's. This summer she asked her mother for one pot on their balcony, all to herself. She chose the seeds, tomato, from a packet at the market, and decided where the pot would go: the sunny corner, not the shady one her mother suggested. Every morning I'd hear her little watering can, and sometimes her voice counting leaves. When the first flower came, she ran down the stairs to show me. When the first tomato turned red, she brought it to me on a steel plate, very serious. "I grew it. I picked the corner," she said. I don't know everything she was thinking, but she stood taller than I'd seen before.

qa.q: Where did Devika decide to put her pot?
qa.a: In the sunny corner, not the shady one her mother suggested.

qa.q: Why does Devika say "I picked the corner" so seriously?
qa.a: She is proud that her own choice worked; the red tomato shows her that what she decided made something happen.

qa.q: What choice by Devika's mother helped Devika learn that her actions matter?
qa.a: Letting Devika choose the seeds and the spot, even against her own suggestion, so the result clearly belonged to Devika.

qa.q: How does Manjula experience Devika's summer?
qa.a: Manjula hears the daily watering and gets shown every stage, and sees Devika standing taller, though only guessing at her thoughts.

grounding: A neighbour watches a child choose and tend a tomato plant and grow more confident when her choice works.

passage:
Saturday: Zubin's remote-control car stopped moving. He handed it to Afreen didi. "Fix it." "You fix it," she said, and gave him a small screwdriver. He poked at it for five minutes and gave up.
Monday: After school Zubin opened the car again, on his own this time. He found a wire loose from the battery box. He pushed it back and pressed it down with tape. The wheels twitched once, then stopped. He frowned, pressed harder, tried again. Whirr. The car shot across the floor.
Thursday: When his friend's torch stopped working, Zubin said, "Let me look," before anyone else could. He opened it, turned the batteries round, and it lit up. He grinned all the way home.

qa.q: What did Zubin find wrong with the car on Monday?
qa.a: A wire loose from the battery box.

qa.q: Why did Zubin say "Let me look" so quickly on Thursday?
qa.a: Fixing the car had shown him his efforts could work, so he felt confident and eager to try again.

qa.q: Which choice by Afreen didi helped Zubin most?
qa.a: Handing him the screwdriver instead of fixing it herself, so the success on Monday was his own.

qa.q: How might Afreen didi feel hearing about the torch on Thursday?
qa.a: She would probably be pleased that saying "You fix it" paid off, seeing her brother now step forward to fix things.

grounding: Over a week a child who fixes his own toy learns his actions matter and offers to fix a friend's torch.

passage: Mehak, come, look at this mango tree. When I was seven, I spat a mango seed into the corner of this yard and asked my father if I could keep it there. He said, "It's yours. You decide." So I decided everything. I put a ring of bricks round it so the goats wouldn't eat it. I carried water from the well in a small brass lota every evening, even when it rained, because I wasn't sure rain counted. When the first two leaves came up, I ran to tell everyone in the lane. Nobody else cared much, but I did. That's when I learned that if I did something, something happened. Disha's tree, they called it. Sixty years, and it still gives mangoes. Now, which pot do you want for your chilli seeds?

qa.q: What did young Disha put round the seed to protect it?
qa.a: A ring of bricks, so the goats wouldn't eat it.

qa.q: Why did young Disha keep watering even when it rained?
qa.a: Disha wasn't sure the rain counted and wanted to be certain the tree got its care; being in charge made every choice feel important.

qa.q: What choice by the father made the lesson possible?
qa.a: Saying "It's yours. You decide", which gave the child real decisions and a result to see.

qa.q: What might Mehak feel when asked to choose a pot for the chilli seeds?
qa.a: Mehak may feel trusted and excited, being handed the same kind of choice that made the mango tree so special.

grounding: An elder recalls how choosing and tending a mango seed as a child showed the child that actions could make things happen.

passage: Ujjwal's kite had torn on the neem tree, and there was no money for a new one before Sankranti. His grandfather, Kishore Dada, handed him a bowl of flour paste, old newspaper and thread. "Your kite. You decide how to fix it." The sun was already low. Ujjwal patched the hole with a big square of newspaper. On the roof the kite dipped and crashed. Too heavy on one side, he thought. He peeled half the patch off, cut a smaller one, and stuck a scrap on the other side to balance it. Dada said nothing, just held the spool. On the second try the kite wobbled, then climbed, steady, just before dark. Ujjwal stared up at it. "I did that," he whispered. "The patch did that."

qa.q: What did Kishore Dada hand Ujjwal?
qa.a: A bowl of flour paste, old newspaper and thread.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's whisper 'I did that' show about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels proud and a bit amazed, seeing that his own decision about the patch is what made the kite fly.

qa.q: What choice by Kishore Dada helped Ujjwal learn that his actions matter?
qa.a: He let Ujjwal decide the repair and stayed quiet even after the crash, so the success clearly came from Ujjwal's own fix.

qa.q: What might Kishore Dada feel watching the kite climb?
qa.a: Probably quiet pride and pleasure, glad he held back his advice so Ujjwal could discover the fix himself.

grounding: A child who decides how to repair his torn kite, and sees it fly after his own adjustment, learns that his actions matter.

passage: In the Chennai flats, Farhan Uncle from the fourth floor gave Ganga, eight, an old plastic bottle made into a bird feeder. "Your job. You choose where it goes." Ganga hung it by the balcony door, where she could see it from her bed. For three days, no birds. Just ants. She sat on the step and thought. The pigeons liked the parapet; she'd seen them. The spot by the door was dark and next to the washing. So she moved the feeder to the sunny corner by the parapet and swept away the ants. On Saturday morning she shouted so loudly that Farhan Uncle looked up from the courtyard: two sparrows, pecking. "I moved it," she told him proudly. "That's why."

qa.q: Where did Ganga first hang the feeder?
qa.a: By the balcony door, where she could see it from her bed.

qa.q: What was Ganga thinking as she sat on the step after three days?
qa.a: She was puzzling out why no birds came, remembering the pigeons on the parapet and noticing that the first spot was dark and next to the washing.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference, and what did Ganga learn from it?
qa.a: Moving the feeder to the sunny corner by the parapet; when the sparrows came, she saw that her own decision had caused it.

qa.q: How might Farhan Uncle feel hearing 'I moved it. That's why'?
qa.a: Farhan Uncle would probably be delighted that giving Ganga the choice paid off, and see how proud she is of working it out herself 😊

grounding: A child chooses where to hang a bird feeder, moves it after it fails, and sees birds come because of her decision.

passage:
"Jasleen didi, can I plant the seed myself?"
"Of course, Deepika. Where do you want to put the pot?"
"Umm... by the window! It's sunny."
"Good choice. How deep?"
"Like this?" Deepika poked her finger into the soil.
"Try it and see."
A week later.
"Didi! Didi! Come see!"
"What happened?"
"A green thing! It came out!"
"You did that. You chose the window."
"Can I plant another one? In the other pot? Maybe on the balcony, to see which one grows faster?"
"That's a great experiment."
"I'll water them every morning. I'll make a chart."
Deepika ran to get her colours.

qa.q: Where did Deepika choose to put the pot?
qa.a: By the window.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel when she saw the sprout?
qa.a: Deepika felt excited and proud, shouting for didi to come and see what had grown from her own choice.

qa.q: How did Jasleen didi help Deepika learn that her actions matter?
qa.a: Jasleen let Deepika make the choices and see the result, then pointed out 'You did that', linking the sprout to Deepika's decision.

qa.q: What is it like for Jasleen didi to watch Deepika plan a second experiment?
qa.a: Jasleen likely feels delighted and a little proud, seeing Deepika grow more confident and curious.

grounding: It shows a child who chooses how to plant a seed and sees it sprout, learning that her actions matter.

passage: When I was ten, my toy car's wheel came off. I wanted to give it to Papa to fix, like always. But my cousin Preeti said, "Try it yourself first." I was annoyed. I thought I'd break it more. I looked at the other wheels. There was a tiny pin in each. The broken one had lost its pin. I found a safety pin in Mummy's sewing box and pushed it through. The wheel wobbled. I bent the pin a little. Then it held. I rolled the car across the whole floor. I kept rolling it just to watch. Now when something breaks, I look first. I'm Sumit, and I still have that car.

qa.q: What did Sumit find in Mummy's sewing box?
qa.a: A safety pin.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when Preeti said to try it alone first?
qa.a: Sumit felt annoyed and worried about breaking the car more.

qa.q: What did Preeti's suggestion do well?
qa.a: It let Sumit decide and see the result, so fixing the wheel became proof that Sumit's actions could change things.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel seeing the car roll across the floor?
qa.a: Preeti may feel pleased and proud that the nudge worked and that Sumit didn't need help.

grounding: It shows a child who fixes a toy without help and sees it work, learning that effort can change things.

passage:
Class 3 note, Friday

Our bird feeder fell and cracked on Monday. Yusuf, who usually waits for instructions, asked if he could fix it. I said yes, and asked how he would do it. He chose tape first. It held for one day, then fell again. On Wednesday he looked at it for a long time and said, "Maybe string, and hang it lower." He tied it himself, a bit crooked. On Thursday two sparrows came. He called everyone to the window, pointing and whispering, "That's my string."

This morning he asked if he could make a second feeder. I'll give him an old bottle and see what he decides.

— Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Yusuf try first to fix the feeder?
qa.a: Tape.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when the sparrows came?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited, calling everyone to the window and whispering 'That's my string.'

qa.q: What did Lakshmi's approach get right?
qa.a: Lakshmi let Yusuf decide how to fix it and try again when it failed, so he could see that his choices changed things.

qa.q: How might Yusuf's classmates see his success?
qa.a: They might be excited and impressed, seeing a quiet classmate take charge and get sparrows to come.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child who decides how to fix a bird feeder and sees it work, learning that his actions matter.

passage:
Sunday
Today I fixed my own cycle chain! It came off again near the temple. Last time Papa fixed it.
This time Amandeep Uncle from next door was washing his car. He said, “You try. I'll just tell you, not do.” So I turned the pedal backwards and put the chain on the small wheel first like he said. It slipped off twice. My hands got black.
The third time it stayed! I rode to the corner and back and it didn't come off.
I told Amma at dinner and she said, “You did that yourself?” and I said YES.
Now I want to fix the squeaky brake too. Uncle says I need a spanner. I'm going to ask Papa for one.
— Minakshi

qa.q: What did Minakshi fix today?
qa.a: Minakshi fixed the cycle chain.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel after the chain stayed on?
qa.a: Minakshi felt proud and excited, telling Amma “YES” at dinner and wanting to fix the brake too.

qa.q: What did Amandeep Uncle do that helped Minakshi's sense of agency?
qa.a: He gave instructions but let Minakshi do it, so the success came from Minakshi's own hands.

qa.q: How might Amma feel hearing the news at dinner?
qa.a: Amma sounded surprised and pleased, asking “You did that yourself?”

grounding: The diary shows a child fixing a cycle chain by their own effort and seeing the result, learning that actions matter.

passage:
In the village near Sangli, it was the first week of the rains. Zainab, eight, asked her mother Uma for a patch of the courtyard.
“For what?”
“To plant.”
Uma gave her a corner by the wall and a handful of okra seeds. “You decide where.”
Zainab chose carefully. She poked five holes with her finger, dropped in the seeds, patted the mud and watered them every evening from a steel lota.
For six days, nothing. She sat by the patch and sulked.
On the seventh morning, she screamed so loud the neighbour's hen ran. Three tiny green loops had pushed up out of the soil.
“Ammi! Mine! I planted them!”
From then on she checked them before brushing her teeth. When one drooped in the sun, she moved a broken pot to shade it. It stood up by evening.

qa.q: How many seeds did Zainab plant?
qa.a: She planted five okra seeds.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel on the seventh morning?
qa.a: She felt thrilled and proud, screaming with joy because the plants were hers.

qa.q: What did Uma do that helped Zainab learn that her actions matter?
qa.a: She let Zainab decide where to plant and care for them herself, so the sprouts were clear evidence of Zainab's own effort.

qa.q: How might Uma feel watching Zainab shade the drooping plant?
qa.a: Uma probably feels proud and touched, seeing her daughter take care of something she started.

grounding: The passage shows a child deciding where to plant seeds, caring for them and seeing them grow, learning that her actions change things.

passage:
In a small flat in Amman, the toy truck Yosef loved had lost a wheel. He brought it to his big sister Nour, holding it out.
“Fix it?”
Nour looked at it. “You fix it. I'll hold the torch.”
Yosef, nine, frowned. He found the wheel under the sofa. He tried pushing it on. It fell off. He tried again. It fell off. He looked at the axle and saw it was bent.
“Can I use your ruler?”
He pressed the axle straight against the ruler, slowly, carefully. Then he pushed the wheel on.
It stayed. He rolled the truck across the tiles, and it went straight.
Yosef looked at the truck, then at his hands. “I did that.”
“You did,” said Nour.
The next week, when the door handle of his cupboard came loose, he went looking for a screwdriver himself.

qa.q: What was wrong with the toy truck's axle?
qa.a: The axle was bent.

qa.q: How did Yosef feel when the truck rolled straight?
qa.a: He felt proud and a bit amazed, looking at his hands and saying “I did that.”

qa.q: What did Nour do that helped build Yosef's agency?
qa.a: She held the torch but let Yosef figure it out and do the fixing, so the success was clearly his.

qa.q: How might Nour feel when Yosef goes looking for a screwdriver the next week?
qa.a: Nour probably feels pleased and proud to see him trying to fix things on his own.

grounding: The passage shows a child fixing a toy himself and seeing the result, learning that his actions matter and trying again later.

passage:
The school garden club met on Wednesdays behind the science block. Ms Vinita handed each child a paper packet of seeds and said, "You choose where to plant. Sun or shade. Near the tap or far. Then we see what happens."
Rekha, nine, walked the whole garden twice. She picked a corner by the wall where the morning sun hit, and she decided to water every Monday and Wednesday herself.
In the second week, nothing. She frowned at the soil. In the third week, a tiny green loop pushed through. Rekha crouched so close her nose nearly touched it. "I did that," she said to nobody. "I picked the sunny spot."
Her friend's seeds, planted in deep shade, were slower. Rekha offered to help move them.
Ms Vinita wrote in her register: Rekha asked today if she could choose the next plant too.

qa.q: Where did Rekha choose to plant her seeds?
qa.a: She picked a corner by the wall where the morning sun hit.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when the green shoot appeared?
qa.a: She felt thrilled and proud, crouching close and saying "I did that", because she could see her choice had worked.

qa.q: Why does letting children choose where to plant help them?
qa.a: Making a choice and then seeing the result gives children evidence that their actions change things, which builds their sense that effort matters.

qa.q: How might Ms Vinita see Rekha after this?
qa.a: Ms Vinita probably sees a child growing in confidence, eager to make the next choice herself.

grounding: It shows a child who decides where to plant and sees her seed sprout, learning from the evidence that her actions matter.

passage:
I'm Kiran, Deepak's older sibling, and I watched this happen over the summer holidays, in the hottest week of May.
Deepak's bicycle chain kept slipping. Usually he'd bring it to Papa and wait. This time Papa was travelling, so Deepak just sat in the shade of the gate staring at the bike.
After a while he fetched the old toolbox. He turned the bike upside down on the veranda, which I'd never seen him do. He tried loosening one bolt, then another. He got oil all over his hands and one cheek. Twice he said something under his breath.
Near sunset he flipped it back, rode to the end of the lane and back. The chain held.
He didn't say anything to me. But the next day, when my torch stopped working, he took it from my hand and opened the battery case before I could ask.

qa.q: What did Deepak do with the bicycle before fixing it?
qa.a: He turned it upside down on the veranda.

qa.q: What does Deepak taking Kiran's torch the next day suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels more confident and capable, having seen that his own effort fixed the bicycle, so he is eager to fix other things.

qa.q: How could the family build on what happened?
qa.a: They could keep giving Deepak small repairs to try himself, instead of fixing things for him, so he keeps collecting evidence that effort works.

qa.q: How does Kiran see the change in Deepak?
qa.a: Kiran notices it with surprise and interest, seeing him try things he'd never done before, though Kiran can't be sure what he is thinking.

grounding: It shows, through a sibling's account, a child who fixes his own bicycle and sees the result, and then tries the next repair himself, as agency grows from evidence.

passage:
Before: In the winter holidays, Noor's wind-up toy car stopped moving. She held it out to her cousin Hrithik. "Fix it." When he said, "You try," she threw it on the bed. "I can't fix things."
During: Two days later, on a foggy morning, Hrithik sat beside her with a small screwdriver. "You decide. Which screw first?" She chose one, then another. Inside was a bent little metal tab. "Should I push it?" she asked. "Your call." She pushed it straight. When she wound the key, the car rolled across the rug.
After: A week later, the kitchen torch went dim. Before anyone could say anything, Noor fetched the screwdriver from Hrithik's box. She opened the back, looked, turned the batteries round and clicked it on. "Fixed," she said, as if it were nothing.

qa.q: What was bent inside the toy car?
qa.a: A little metal tab was bent inside.

qa.q: How did Noor feel about fixing things before the toy car?
qa.a: She felt helpless and frustrated, throwing the car on the bed and saying she couldn't fix things.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that helped Noor, and why?
qa.a: He let her decide each step, which screw and whether to push the tab, so the fixed car became her own evidence that her actions work.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel seeing Noor fix the torch alone?
qa.a: Hrithik would likely feel proud and pleased that she now tries repairs herself without asking.

grounding: It shows a child who makes the choices while fixing a toy and sees it work, then fixes a torch on her own, as agency grows from evidence.

passage:
Simran, you see that jamun tree by the gate? Your Uday Dadaji planted it when he was nine. That monsoon my father gave me a seed and said, "You choose where it goes." I chose that corner, where rainwater ran off the roof. Every day after school I checked. Nothing. Two weeks, nothing. I almost gave up.
Then one morning, a little green loop pushing through the mud. I shouted so loudly the neighbours came. I chose the spot, I watered it, and it grew. After that, when my cycle chain broke, I didn't cry for my father. I tried fixing it myself.
So, beta, which pot do you want for your tulsi? You choose.

qa.q: Where did young Uday plant the jamun seed?
qa.a: In the corner by the gate where rainwater ran off the roof.

qa.q: How did young Uday feel when the green loop appeared?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and proud, shouting so loudly the neighbours came, because his own choice and care had made it grow.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: His father letting him choose the spot; seeing his choice and watering produce a shoot taught him his actions mattered, so later he tried fixing his cycle chain himself.

qa.q: How might Uday's father have felt watching the seed come up?
qa.a: His father probably felt quietly pleased, having handed over the choice on purpose and seeing his son learn that effort changes things.

grounding: An elder recalls choosing where to plant a seed as a child and seeing it grow, which taught him that his actions mattered.
